topics.title: Summing and difference amplifiers
topics.summary: Add several inputs with an inverting summer; subtract two with a difference amplifier that rejects what they have in common.

lensNotes.circuit: Summing works because the virtual ground adds the input currents. The difference amplifier subtracts, but only as well as its resistor pairs match.
lensNotes.signals: Mixers, DAC outputs, and offset adders are summers. Difference amplifiers reject noise common to both wires (common mode), which is how sensor signals survive long cables.

prerequisiteNotes.opamp_inverting: A summing amplifier is several inverting amplifiers sharing one virtual ground, and their currents add there.
prerequisiteNotes.opamp_noninverting: A difference amplifier combines both paths: one input sees the inverting gain, the other the non-inverting gain through a divider.

goals: Find the output of an inverting summer from each input voltage and its resistor
Choose input resistors to give each input of a summer its own gain
Find a difference amplifier's output with matched resistor pairs, and explain why a voltage common to both inputs cancels
Explain why changing one input resistor of a summer leaves the other inputs' currents unchanged
topics.intuition: A summer adds currents at its virtual ground: each input sends its own V/R, and Rf turns the total into the output. A difference amplifier gives V1 and V2 equal and opposite gains, so whatever they share cancels, but only as far as its two resistor pairs match. Both circuits need negative feedback and an output inside the op amp's swing limits.
topics.why: In the summer, with the + input grounded, feedback holds the summing node at 0 V. Each input resistor has its source on one end and 0 V on the other, so its current is V_n/R_n, whatever the other inputs do. None enters the op amp, so by KCL they add in Rf: Vout = −Rf × their sum. In the difference amplifier, take one input at a time. With V2 at 0 V, V1 meets an inverting stage with gain −Rf/R. V2 passes a divider (R on top, Rf to ground) to reach the + input as V2·Rf/(R + Rf), then the non-inverting gain 1 + Rf/R makes it exactly V2·Rf/R. A shared voltage cancels; a resistor mismatch lets some through.
topics.explanation: Start from the inverting amplifier. Its − input is a virtual ground, so the current through Rin is Vin/Rin. Connect a second input through its own resistor to the same node. The node stays at 0 V, so each input sends its own current, V1/R1 and V2/R2, and neither affects the other. No current enters the op amp, so the currents add up in Rf: Vout = −Rf·(V1/R1 + V2/R2). Each input has its own gain, −Rf/R_n, and each source sees just its own R_n. To subtract, combine both amplifiers. V1 goes through R to the − input, with Rf as feedback: the inverting path. V2 goes through a matching divider, R then Rf to ground, into the + input: the non-inverting path. With both pairs matched, Vout = (Rf/R)·(V2 − V1). Here the − input sits at V+, not at 0 V: no virtual ground. V2's source sees R + Rf. V1's current, (V1 − V+)/R, depends on V2 as well, so V1 has no fixed input resistance. A voltage added to both inputs, such as a ground difference along a cable, cancels: common-mode rejection. It is only as good as the resistor match.

workedExample.problem: Two stages run from ±15 V supplies. (a) An inverting summer has Rf = 47 kΩ, with V1 = 0.60 V through R1 = 10 kΩ and V2 = 1.20 V through R2 = 22 kΩ. Find its output. (b) A difference amplifier has R = 10 kΩ on both inputs and Rf = 100 kΩ for the feedback and the ground leg, with V1 = 2.45 V on the inverting side and V2 = 2.55 V on the non-inverting side. Find its output, then add 1.00 V to both inputs.
steps: (a) The + input is grounded, so the summing node is a virtual ground at 0 V. Input currents: I1 = 0.60 V / 10 kΩ = 60.0 µA and I2 = 1.20 V / 22 kΩ = 54.5 µA.

(a) Both currents flow on through Rf: 60.0 µA + 54.5 µA = 114.5 µA, so Vout = −47 kΩ × 114.5 µA = −5.38 V, inside ±15 V. Each input has its own gain: −47 kΩ / 10 kΩ = −4.7 for V1 and −47 kΩ / 22 kΩ = −2.14 for V2.
(b) The + input draws no current, so V+ = 2.55 V × 100 kΩ / (10 kΩ + 100 kΩ) = 2.3182 V, and feedback makes V− = 2.3182 V: not 0 V.

(b) Current in V1's 10 kΩ input resistor: (2.45 V − 2.3182 V) / 10 kΩ = 13.18 µA toward the − input. All of it flows on through Rf, dropping 13.18 µA × 100 kΩ = 1.318 V, so Vout = 2.3182 V − 1.3182 V = 1.00 V.
(b) Check with the formula: Vout = (100 kΩ / 10 kΩ) × (2.55 V − 2.45 V) = 10 × 0.10 V = 1.00 V, inside ±15 V.

(b) Add 1.00 V to both: V1 = 3.45 V, V2 = 3.55 V. V+ = 3.55 V × 100 kΩ / 110 kΩ = 3.2273 V; the current in V1's R is (3.45 V − 3.2273 V) / 10 kΩ = 22.27 µA, and Vout = 3.2273 V − 22.27 µA × 100 kΩ = 3.2273 V − 2.2273 V = 1.00 V again: the shared 1.00 V cancels.
Input resistance: in (a) each source sees only its own resistor, 10 kΩ and 22 kΩ. In (b) V2's source sees 10 kΩ + 100 kΩ = 110 kΩ.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 8 "Operational Amplifiers", section "Averager and summer circuits"
sources.note: In the inverting summer, each input current is set by its own voltage and resistor into the virtual ground, the currents add in the feedback resistor, and the output is their inverted sum.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Operational Amplifiers" (last update 23 September 2026), section 3.12 "Differential amplification" (pp. 65–69)
sources.note: Superposition shows that the four-resistor subtractor gives Vout = V+ − V− with equal resistors and other gains from the resistor ratios; the + input voltage comes from an unloaded divider, and the + source sees both lower resistors in series.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 8 "Operational Amplifiers", section "Practical considerations", subsection "Common-mode gain"
sources.note: An ideal differential amplifier ignores a voltage shared by both inputs, and a mismatch among the external resistors creates common-mode gain that only rebalancing them removes.

templates.prompt: An inverting summer (op amp on ±15 V supplies, not drawn) has Rf = {Rf}. Input {V1} arrives through R1 = {R1} and input {V2} through R2 = {R2}. What is the output voltage?
templates.explanation: The inverting input is a virtual ground, so each input sends its own current: {I1} and {I2}. Both flow through Rf: Vout = −Rf·(V1/R1 + V2/R2) = {answer}.
hints: Each input resistor sees its input voltage on one end and 0 V on the other.
Add the currents, then Vout = −Rf × (total current).

misconceptions.feedback: Vout = −(V1 + V2) only when all three resistors are equal. Weight each input by Rf/R: Vout = −Rf·(V1/R1 + V2/R2).

steps: The inverting input is a virtual ground (0 V).
Input 1 pushes {I1} through R1; input 2 pushes {I2} through R2.
No current enters the op amp, so both currents flow on through Rf.

followUps.prompt: Both inputs meet at the same node. Why doesn't input 1's voltage change the current that flows in from input 2?

choices.text: Feedback holds the node at 0 V (a virtual ground), so each input's current is just its own V/R
choices.feedback: Right: current 2 is V2/R2 whatever V1 does. The currents only meet at the node and add up in Rf.

choices.text: The op amp's inputs have infinite resistance, which keeps the two inputs apart
choices.feedback: Infinite input resistance means no current goes into the op amp. What keeps the inputs apart is that their shared node is held at 0 V.

choices.text: It does change it, but the changes cancel in Rf
choices.feedback: Nothing needs to cancel: with the node held at 0 V, each current depends only on its own voltage and resistor.

choices.text: Each input has its own feedback path through Rf
choices.feedback: There is only one Rf, and both currents flow through it. That's why they add.

followUps.explanation: Two ideas from earlier: the virtual ground (from the inverting amplifier) keeps the node at 0 V, so Ohm's law gives each current separately; Kirchhoff's current law then says both currents leave through Rf, so their effects add. Without the virtual ground, the inputs would pull on each other like resistors joined at a node.

templates.prompt: A difference amplifier (op amp on ±15 V supplies, not drawn) uses R = {R} on both inputs and Rf = {Rf} for both the feedback and the ground leg. V1 = {V1} goes to the inverting side and V2 = {V2} to the non-inverting side. What is the output?
templates.explanation: With matched resistor pairs, Vout = (Rf/R)(V2 − V1) = {G} × ({V2} − {V1}) = {answer}. Anything common to both inputs cancels.
hints: Which input is subtracted from which?
Vout = (Rf / R) · (V2 − V1), where V2 is the non-inverting input.

misconceptions.feedback: A difference amplifier subtracts: Vout = (Rf/R)(V2 − V1).

steps: The difference between the inputs: V2 − V1 = {V2} − {V1} = {dV}.
With matched ratios, the output amplifies only the difference: V_out = (Rf/R)·(V2 − V1).

followUps.prompt: Why must the two resistor ratios match (Rf/R1 on the inverting side equal to R4/R3, the ground leg over the series resistor, on the non-inverting side) for a voltage common to both inputs to cancel?

choices.text: Only with matched ratios do V1's path and V2's path (a divider, then a non-inverting gain) have the same size of gain
choices.feedback: Right: with matched pairs, V2 gets (Rf/(R + Rf))·(1 + Rf/R) = Rf/R, exactly the size of V1's gain. A mismatch makes the two gains differ, and a common voltage leaks through.

choices.text: Matched resistors draw equal currents from both inputs, and the currents cancel inside the op amp
choices.feedback: No current flows into the op-amp inputs, so nothing can cancel inside it. The cancellation happens because the two paths have equal gains.

choices.text: Matching only sets the overall gain; a common voltage cancels whatever the resistors are
choices.feedback: With a mismatch, V1 and V2 see different gains, so the same voltage on both gives a nonzero output.

choices.text: Matching keeps the output away from the rails when both inputs are high
choices.feedback: Staying inside the rails is about the size of the signal. Matching is what makes the two input paths have the same gain.

followUps.explanation: The difference amplifier is two amplifiers in one: V1 sees an inverting amplifier (gain −Rf/R), and V2 sees a divider (from Foundations) followed by a non-inverting amplifier. With matched pairs both gains are Rf/R in size, so Vout = (Rf/R)(V2 − V1), and anything common to both inputs cancels.

templates.prompt: An ideal difference amplifier with matched resistors (gain {G}) has {Vcm} applied to both inputs at once. What is the output?

choices.feedback: Right: the amplifier only responds to the difference, and the difference is zero.
The common voltage cancels; only V2 − V1 is amplified.
That would amplify the common-mode voltage. A matched difference amplifier rejects it.
No: the inputs are equal, so there's nothing to amplify.

templates.explanation: Vout = G(V2 − V1) = G × 0 = 0 V. Rejecting what both inputs share (common-mode rejection) is what makes difference amplifiers useful for noisy sensor wiring.

templates.prompt: An inverting summer uses Rf = {Rf}. What input resistor R1 gives input 1 a gain of −{G}? Give the exact value (you would then fit the nearest E24 part).
templates.explanation: Each input of an inverting summer has its own gain −Rf/R_n. For −{G}: R1 = Rf/{G} = {Rf}/{G} = {answer}. Then pick the nearest E24 value; the gain moves by the same few percent by which the part differs from the exact value.
hints: Each input sees its own inverting amplifier into the virtual ground.

misconceptions.feedback: Bigger R1 means less current and less gain. R1 = Rf/G.

templates.prompt: Inputs of {V1}, {V2}, and {V3} each go through their own input resistor into an inverting summer (op amp on ±15 V supplies, not drawn). Every input resistor and the feedback resistor are {R}. What is the output voltage?
templates.explanation: With every resistor equal, each input has a gain of −1, so V_out = −(V1 + V2 + V3). The inputs add to {V1} + {V2} + ({V3}) = {sum}, so V_out = {answer}.
hints: What is the gain of each input when R_n = Rf?
V_out = −(V1 + V2 + V3) when all resistors match.

misconceptions.feedback: The summer inverts: V_out = −(V1 + V2 + V3).
Keep V3's sign: it is already negative.

templates.prompt: An inverting summer (op amp on ±15 V supplies, not drawn) has Rf = {Rf}. Input 1 ({V1}) arrives through R1 = {R1}, and input 2 ({V2}) through R2 = {R2}. R1 is swapped for {new_R1}. What happens to the current flowing in through R2?

feedback.up: Less current from input 1 doesn't leave more room for input 2: the summing node isn't sharing a fixed current. It is held at 0 V, so input 2's current is V2/R2 whatever R1 is.
feedback.down: R1 and R2 aren't in series, and they don't share a voltage drop. The summing node stays at 0 V, so R2 still has {V2} across it.

templates.explanation: The current through R2 stays at V2/R2 = {after}. The summing node is a virtual ground, so each input resistor has its own source on one end and 0 V on the other. Changing R1 changes only input 1's current, and with it the output; input 2 doesn't notice. That independence is why a summer can mix signals without them interfering.
hints: What voltage sits at the node where R1 and R2 meet?

templates.prompt: An inverting summer (op amp on ±15 V supplies, not drawn) has Rf = {Rf}. Input 1 ({V1}) arrives through R1 = {R1}, and input 2 ({V2}) through R2 = {R2}. R1 is swapped for {new_R1}. What happens to the size of the output voltage?

whatIf.quantity: the size of the output voltage

feedback.up: A bigger resistor gives a bigger voltage only when the same current flows through it. Here the bigger R1 lets less current in from input 1, so less current flows through Rf.
feedback.same: The output is Rf times the total current into the summing node, and input 1's share, V1/R1, drops to a tenth.

templates.explanation: |Vout| = Rf·(V1/R1 + V2/R2) goes from {before} to {after}. Input 1's current falls to a tenth; input 2's current doesn't change (the node stays at 0 V). So the output shrinks, but not to a tenth: input 2's part is still there.
hints: Each input's current is V/R into a node held at 0 V. Which current changes?

templates.prompt: A difference amplifier (op amp on ±15 V supplies, not drawn) with matched pairs (R = {R} on both inputs, Rf = {Rf} for the feedback and the ground leg) has V1 = {V1} on the inverting side and V2 = {V2} on the non-inverting side. A ground difference along a long cable adds the same 1 V to both inputs: V1 becomes {new_V1} and V2 becomes {new_V2}. What happens to the output voltage?

feedback.up: Both inputs went up, but the amplifier only sees their difference, and V2 − V1 hasn't changed.
feedback.down: The extra volt on V1 pushes the output down, but the same volt on V2 pushes it up by exactly as much, because the matched pairs give both inputs the same size of gain.

templates.explanation: Vout = (Rf/R)(V2 − V1) stays at {after}. The ground difference raises V1 and V2 by the same amount, so V2 − V1 is unchanged: V1's path (gain −Rf/R) and V2's path (a divider, then a gain of 1 + Rf/R, also Rf/R overall) cancel it exactly. This common-mode rejection is why difference amplifiers read sensors over long wires.
hints: Work out V2 − V1 before and after.

templates.prompt: This two-input inverting summer runs from ±12 V supplies (rail-to-rail output, not drawn). Input 1 ({V1}) goes through R1 = {R1}, input 2 ({V2}) through R2 = {R2}, and Rf = {Rf}. The output should be {h0}. The meter readings are below. Which fault explains them?

faults.feedback: With R1 open, input 1 would send no current (0 A in R1), while input 2 kept its normal current. The output would be input 2's share alone, −Rf·V2/R2.
faults.why: R1 carries no current, while R2 still carries its normal V2/R2, so the summing node still works. The output is smaller than it should be: it is input 2's share alone, −Rf·V2/R2. Input 1 is cut off at R1.

faults.feedback: With R2 open, input 2 would send no current (0 A in R2), while input 1 kept its normal current. The output would be input 1's share alone, −Rf·V1/R1.
faults.why: R2 carries no current, while R1 still carries its normal V1/R1. The output is input 1's share alone, −Rf·V1/R1. Input 2 is cut off at R2.

faults.feedback: With Rf open, the input currents would have nowhere to go but from one input into the other. The summing node would no longer sit at 0 V, and the op amp, with no feedback, would drive its output to the −12 V rail.
faults.why: The output sits at the −12 V rail: nothing feeds back, so the summing node floats up to a voltage between the two inputs, and the op amp, seeing V− above V+, saturates. R1 and R2 now carry the same small current in opposite directions (one meter reads negative): current flows from the higher input through both resistors into the lower one, and none if the inputs are equal.

faults.text: Rf is shorted (a solder bridge across it)
faults.feedback: With Rf shorted, the output would be tied to the summing node, which feedback holds at 0 V: the output would read 0 V while both inputs kept their normal currents, flowing into the bridge.
faults.why: Both input currents are normal, so the summing node is still held at 0 V. But the output reads 0 V: the combined current flows through the Rf position without dropping any voltage, so Rf is bridged.

templates.explanation: First look at the output: if it sits at a rail, the feedback path is broken (Rf open). Otherwise, read the input currents: each one is V/R into a virtual ground. If one is zero, that input is cut off, and the output shows only the other input's share. If both are normal but the output is 0 V, the current is getting back without a drop (Rf bridged).
hints: Look at the output first: is it at a rail?
If not, check the two input currents: is either of them zero, or are both normal?

templates.prompt: A difference amplifier (ideal op amp on ±12 V supplies, not drawn) subtracts a 2.5 V reference, V1, from a sensor's voltage, V2. The reference comes from a buffer with negligible output resistance; the sensor behaves as a voltage source behind its own output resistance, R_s = {Rs}. R1 = {R1} and R_f = {Rf} give V1 a gain of −{G}, and R4 = {Rf} is fitted as R_f's matched partner. Choose R3 (E24, 1 kΩ to 100 kΩ) so that V2's gain is +{G} within 0.4%: then a volt common to both inputs moves the output by at most {cmMax}. Treat the resistors as exact (in practice, 0.1% parts).
templates.explanation: V2 reaches the + input through a divider: the + input draws no current, so V+ = V2 × R4/(R_s + R3 + R4). The sensor's own R_s is in series with R3, part of the divider's top. The non-inverting gain 1 + R_f/R1 = {Gn} then gives V2 a gain of {Gn} × R4/(R_s + R3 + R4). That equals V1's {G} exactly when R4/(R_s + R3) = R_f/R1, the matched-pair condition with R_s counted. With R4 = R_f, the top of the divider must total R1: R3 = {R1} − {Rs} = {R3ex}. Fitting R3 = R1, as if the sensor had no resistance, gives V2 a gain of {Gtrap} instead of {G}, so each volt common to both inputs leaks through as {CMtrap} at the output. In practice R_s also drifts with temperature, which is why sensors with real output resistance are usually buffered first (the front of an instrumentation amplifier).
hints: Which resistances lie between the sensor's ideal voltage and the + input? R_s is one of them.
V2's gain is (1 + R_f/R1) × R4/(R_s + R3 + R4). It equals R_f/R1 when R4/(R_s + R3) = R_f/R1.

followUps.prompt: Why does the sensor's output resistance spoil the rejection of a voltage common to both inputs?

choices.text: R_s adds to R3 in V2's divider, so V2's gain no longer equals V1's, and a common voltage no longer cancels
choices.feedback: Right: cancellation needs the two inputs' gains to be equal and opposite. R_s changes only V2's side, so the two gains differ and a share of any common voltage reaches the output.

choices.text: Current flows from the sensor into the + input through R_s, adding an error at the output
choices.feedback: The + input draws no current. Current flows from the sensor down through R_s, R3, and R4 to ground, and R_s simply becomes part of that divider.

choices.text: R_s only lowers the overall gain; the rejection of a common voltage is unaffected
choices.feedback: Rejection depends on the two inputs having equal gains. R_s lowers V2's gain alone, so the gains differ and a common voltage leaks through.

choices.text: R_s matters only for the inverting input, where the virtual ground draws current from the source
choices.feedback: Here R_s is on the non-inverting side, and the − input is not at 0 V in a difference amplifier anyway. On V2's side R_s is in series with R3 and changes the divider ratio.

followUps.explanation: A difference amplifier rejects a common voltage only because V1's path (gain −R_f/R1) and V2's path (a divider, then 1 + R_f/R1) have exactly equal sizes of gain. Any resistance in series with one input changes that input's ratio: with R3 = R1 it would leak {CMtrap} per volt of common-mode signal, against the {cmMax} allowed. Counting R_s inside R3 restores the match; an instrumentation amplifier avoids the problem by buffering each input so the source resistance doesn't matter.

schematic.noBuild: R_s is the sensor's own output resistance, a model of the source, not a part
